title: Contraction of the iterated DG cone for two composable maps
statement: Work in the universes of [def-weil-size-convention]. A differential graded algebra over $\mathbf Z$ means an associative unital graded ring $A=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbf Z}A^i$ with additive differential $d:A^i\to A^{i+1}$ satisfying $d^2=0$ and $d(ab)=d(a)b+(-1)^ia\,d(b)$ for $a\in A^i$. A right differential graded $A$-module is a graded right module $M$ with $d^2=0$ and $d(ma)=d(m)a+(-1)^jm\,d(a)$ for $m\in M^j$. Write $K_A$ for the category of these modules with degree-preserving $A$-linear chain maps modulo homotopies $f-g=dh+hd$, where $h$ is $A$-linear of degree $-1$. Shifts have $M[k]^i=M^{i+k}$, differential $(-1)^kd_M$, and the unchanged right action. For a chain map $f:X\to Y$, put $C(f)^i=Y^i\oplus X^{i+1}$, $d_{C(f)}(y,x)=(d_Yy+f(x),-d_Xx)$, with componentwise right action. Put $i_f(y)=(y,0)$ and $p_f(y,x)=x$. Write $T_f$ for the triangle $X\xrightarrow fY\xrightarrow{i_f}C(f)\xrightarrow{-p_f}X[1]$ in $K_A$. For composable chain maps $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$, set $\alpha:C(f)\to C(gf)$, $\alpha(y,x)=(g(y),x)$, $\beta:C(gf)\to C(g)$, $\beta(z,x)=(z,f(x))$, and $\gamma:C(g)\to C(f)[1]$, $\gamma(z,y)=(-y,0)$. These are $A$-linear chain maps. There is an isomorphism of triangles in $K_A$ from $T_\alpha$ to $(C(f),C(gf),C(g),\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ whose first two components are identities. Its third component is represented, in coordinates $C(\alpha)^n=Z^n\oplus X^{n+1}\oplus Y^{n+1}\oplus X^{n+2}$, by $r(z,x,y,t)=(z,f(x)+y)$. The chain map $s(z,y)=(z,0,y,0)$ is a homotopy inverse of $r$, and $r i_\alpha=\beta$ and $\gamma r=-p_\alpha$ in $K_A$.

proof.text: Use the shifts and cones defined in the statement. For any chain map $u:M\to N$, the cone differential squares to zero since its off-diagonal entry is $d_Nu-ud_M=0$; its Leibniz rule follows from those of $M,N$, with $(-1)^{n+1}$ on the shifted summand cancelling the minus differential. The unchanged shifted action satisfies the same rule since $(-1)^k(-1)^{n+k}=(-1)^n$. Thus all displayed cones and shifts are right DG modules. The maps $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ preserve degrees and are $A$-linear. The two sides of their chain-map equations, evaluated on $(y,x),(z,x),(z,y)$ respectively, are $(g d_Yy+gf(x),-d_Xx)$, $(d_Zz+gf(x),-f(d_Xx))$, and $(d_Yy,0)$. Here only $d_Yf=fd_X$ and $d_Zg=gd_Y$ were used.

source.place: Definitions definition-shift, definition-homotopy, definition-cone; Tag 09KI (lemma-two-split-injections), concrete cone coordinates.

proof.text: Write $D=d_{C(\alpha)}$. Expanding the cone gives $D(z,x,y,t)=(d_Zz+gf(x)+g(y),-d_Xx+t,-d_Yy-f(t),d_Xt)$. Both $r$ and $s$ in the statement are degree-preserving and $A$-linear. Direct substitution gives $rD=d_{C(g)}r=(d_Zz+g(f(x)+y),-f(d_Xx)-d_Yy)$ and $Ds=s d_{C(g)}=(d_Zz+g(y),0,-d_Yy,0)$. Thus $r$ and $s$ are chain maps, and $rs=1$ strictly.

Define the degree $-1$ graded $A$-linear map $H:C(\alpha)\to C(\alpha)$ by $H(z,x,y,t)=(0,0,0,x)$. Its last coordinate belongs to $X^{n+1}$ in degree $n-1$. The formula for $D$ gives $DH=(0,x,-f(x),d_Xx)$ and $HD=(0,0,0,-d_Xx+t)$. Consequently $DH+HD=(0,x,-f(x),t)=1-sr$. Together with $rs=1$, this exhibits $s$ as a homotopy inverse of $r$ using precisely the $A$-linear homotopies defining $K_A$.

The second triangle square commutes strictly: $r i_\alpha(z,x)=(z,f(x))=\beta(z,x)$. For the last square, $\gamma r(z,x,y,t)=(-f(x)-y,0)$ whereas $-p_\alpha(z,x,y,t)=(-y,-t)$. Define the degree $-1$ graded $A$-linear map $J:C(\alpha)\to C(f)[1]$ by $J(z,x,y,t)=(0,x)$. Since $d_{C(f)[1]}(a,b)=(-d_Ya-f(b),d_Xb)$, we have $d_{C(f)[1]}J+JD=(-f(x),d_Xx)+(0,-d_Xx+t)=(-f(x),t)=\gamma r-(-p_\alpha)$. Hence the last square commutes in $K_A$.

source.place: Tag 09KF (lemma-the-same-up-to-isomorphisms), proof (1), final square with -p; Tag 09KI (lemma-two-split-injections), connecting composite.

proof.text: The triple $(1_{C(f)},1_{C(gf)},[r])$ now satisfies all three triangle-morphism equations: the first is $\alpha=\alpha$, and the other two were just proved. It is invertible: $(1,1,[s])$ is its inverse because $[r][s]=1$ and $[s][r]=1$. The inverse's square equations also follow by composing those for $[r]$ with $[s]$. This is the required isomorphism of triangles with the specified first two identities and third representative.
